references.text: John's Revelation describes the abyss (ἄβυσσος) as a place where evil spirits are imprisoned. The demons in Luke 8:31 beg Jesus not to send them there, showing that the abyss is a feared place of punishment for evil spiritual powers.
Satan is cast into the abyss and bound there for a thousand years. This confirms the abyss as a prison for evil spiritual powers, just as the demons in Luke 8:31 feared being sent there.
In Matthew's parallel account, the demons cry out, "Have you come here to torment us before the time?" This expresses the same fear as in Luke 8:31, where they beg not to be sent to the abyss.
Mark's parallel account tells that the unclean spirits begged Jesus not to send them away from the area and asked to be allowed to enter the pigs – the same event as in Luke 8:31-33.

Peter writes that God did not spare angels who had sinned, but cast them down into the abyss (tartarus) where they are held in custody until judgment. This shows that the abyss is a place of punishment for fallen spiritual powers, just as the demons feared.

Jude writes about angels who did not keep their high position and whom God holds in custody in darkness with eternal chains until the judgment on the great day. This confirms that evil spiritual powers can be bound and imprisoned, just as the demons in Luke 8:31 feared.

The context immediately before: the possessed man falls down before Jesus and cries out with a loud voice, recognizing him as "the Son of the Most High God". The demons' plea not to be sent to the abyss in verse 31 follows directly from this recognition of Jesus' divine authority.
The beast that rises from the abyss is linked to the same concept (ἄβυσσος) that the demons feared in Luke 8:31, showing the abyss as a dwelling place for evil powers.

Paul uses the term "the abyss" (ἄβυσσος) in a rhetorical context: "Who will descend into the abyss?" – meaning to bring Christ up from the dead. The use of the same word connects it to the idea of the abyss as a deep, inaccessible place.
